I think therein lies the crux of the issue. The SCOTUS is supposed to make rulings based on the Constitution as written. Meaning "Is <law> allowed under the Constitution?" If the answer is "no", then the law must be struck down, no matter how people feel about it.

What happens from time to time, however, is you get one or several "activist judges" who feel it's their duty to interpret the Constitution based on some nebulous idea of it being a "living document", that changes with the times. The problem with that is doing so is completely against the spirit of the Constitution in the first place. There are very specific guidelines set forth for making amendments, and none of them involve upholding laws just because people think "it's time for this to happen."

The problem with that arises with things like the current attacks on the Second Amendment. The gun-grabbers want to argue til the cows come home about technicalities, loopholes, the intent of the framers, etc. But the fact of the matter is, it explicitly states that "A well regulated militia being necessary to the security of a free state, the right of the people to keep and bear arms shall not be infringed."

Leftist like to argue that the first part means government regulation. It does not. At the time the document was written, people used the term "well regulated" to mean "functions properly and efficiently." Therefore, a well regulated militia is one that is prepared, able, and willing to carry out its duties whenever the need should arise. Key to this was the right of every citizen to keep and bear arms.

Now what SHOULD happen if people REALLY want to make guns illegal, is get enough support to convene a Constitutional Convention, pass an amendment that would effectively repeal the Second Amendment, and then have it be ratified by each state. But the gun-grabbers know this will never happen, so they continue trying to do end-runs around the Constitution with things like "assault weapon" bans, activist judges, etc.

If the SCOTUS is ruling based on "social justice" or making decisions because it's the "right" thing to do in "the current year", then they're not doing their job to uphold the Constitution. Their only job is to look at a case before them and decide "is the matter presented to us in accordance with the Constitution as written." Period. End of story.
They also look at decades, mayhaps centuries of prior case law, which is a pretty BFD you may be overlooking.
